_comment: A small workspace and the questions it can answer, committed so every eval run on
every machine measures the same thing. Written by hand rather than harvested,
because a golden set drawn from one person's approvals inherits their habits.
The notes are deliberately uneven, the way real ones are: some pages are careful
prose, some are a line of shorthand written at speed, two of them disagree with
each other, and one records a price that has since changed. Every case below names
the property it tests in `why`, so a failure says what broke rather than which

blocks.text: Scaled dot-product attention divides the logits by the square root of the key dimension. Without that divisor the dot products grow with dimension and push the softmax into a region where gradients vanish.
Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel over different learned projections and concatenates their outputs before a final linear map.
Attention is quadratic in sequence length because every position attends to every other, which is what makes long contexts expensive rather than merely slow.
Grouped-query attention shares key and value projections across several query heads, which cuts the size of the KV cache at a small quality cost.

AdamW decouples weight decay from the gradient update. Adam with L2 regularisation folds the penalty into the gradient, where the adaptive denominator then scales it differently for every parameter, which is not what weight decay is supposed to mean.
Learning-rate warmup exists because the adaptive moment estimates are unreliable in the first few hundred steps, when they have seen too few gradients to be trusted.
Gradient clipping by global norm is the standard remedy for loss spikes in large runs. Clipping per parameter changes the update direction and is worse.
Pre-norm transformers put layer normalisation inside the residual branch. This makes deep stacks trainable without warmup, at some cost to final quality compared with post-norm.
RMSNorm drops the mean-centring step of LayerNorm and keeps only the rescaling, which is cheaper and works about as well in practice.
A linear probe that recovers a feature from a hidden state shows the feature is linearly decodable there. It does not show the network uses it.
The CKA/RSA stuff from last term is worth another pass before the exam — I never properly followed the derivation.
Sparse autoencoders decompose activations into an overcomplete dictionary of features, on the theory that superposition packs more features into a layer than it has dimensions.
The Chinchilla result is that for a fixed compute budget, parameters and training tokens should grow at roughly the same rate. Earlier models were badly undertrained for their size.
Apparent emergent abilities at scale are often an artefact of a discontinuous metric. Measured with a smooth one, the same capability improves gradually.
Continuous batching keeps the accelerator busy by admitting new sequences as old ones finish, instead of waiting for a whole batch to complete.
Paged attention stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks so that memory is not fragmented by sequences of different lengths.
Eight-bit weight quantisation is close to free in quality terms. Four-bit needs care and usually some form of outlier handling.
Claude Opus 5 costs five dollars per million input tokens and twenty-five dollars per million output tokens on the first-party API.
Prompt caching bills cache reads at roughly a tenth of the input rate, which is what makes a long stable system prompt affordable across many calls.
Still to read: the paged attention paper, the original Chinchilla paper, and whatever the current best survey of sparse autoencoders is.
Does the layer-9 probing result hold on Qwen2.5, or is it specific to Llama? Nobody in the group has checked.
Is warmup still necessary with pre-norm and a well-tuned optimiser, or is it cargo cult at this point?
Benchmark contamination is the default assumption now. A score on a public benchmark is evidence about the benchmark, not about the model.
Pairwise human preference is noisy but unbiased; a single-model rubric score is less noisy and quietly biased towards whatever the rubric author liked.

retrieval.query: why divide attention logits by the square root of the key dimension
retrieval.why: Plain vocabulary overlap. If this fails, BM25 itself is broken.

retrieval.query: why does decoupling the weight decay term help generalisation
retrieval.why: Same concept, most content words shared. Lexical retrieval should still reach it.

retrieval.query: representational similarity analysis between two networks
retrieval.why: The note wrote the acronym; the source spells it out. No shared token at all, so this is unreachable lexically and is the case embeddings exist for.

retrieval.query: reducing the memory taken by cached keys and values during generation
retrieval.why: Two pages legitimately cover this. Recall over both matters more than which ranks first.
The page title carries the answer and no block repeats the phrase. Tests the title boost.

retrieval.query: gradient clipping by global norm for loss spikes
retrieval.why: Must beat the many other pages that mention gradients.

retrieval.query: what does a linear probe actually demonstrate
retrieval.why: The block's point is a caveat. Retrieval must not prefer a page that merely mentions probing.

retrieval.query: how much does opus cost per million output tokens
retrieval.why: Numbers and product names, the shape of a fact lookup.

retrieval.query: has anyone checked whether that result transfers to Qwen
retrieval.why: Questions are content too; the sweep that surfaces them depends on this.

retrieval.query: how should parameters and tokens scale together for a compute budget
retrieval.why: Concept stated without naming the paper.

retrieval.query: is int8 quantisation lossy in practice
retrieval.why: The note says eight-bit, the query says int8 — a vocabulary gap a reranker can close.

retrieval.query: does putting layernorm inside the residual branch remove the need for warmup
retrieval.why: Spans two pages; the normalisation page should lead.

retrieval.query: why does one neuron respond to several unrelated concepts at once
retrieval.why: The note calls this superposition and never uses the word neuron. Second unreachable-lexically case, so the semantic score is not resting on one example.

retrieval.query: is it worth training a smaller model past the compute-optimal point
retrieval.why: Competes with every other page that mentions training.

retrieval.query: are automatic rubric scores biased compared with asking people to compare two answers
retrieval.why: Long query with several near-miss pages; tests that length does not dilute the match.

retrieval.query: what makes very long prompts expensive
retrieval.why: Two defensible answers — the quadratic cost and the token price. Either is a hit; returning neither is not.

relations.claim: Speculative decoding drafts several tokens with a small model and verifies them in one pass of the large one.
relations.why: Nothing in the workspace covers speculative decoding. The nearest page is about serving, so a lazy classifier will reach for corroborates.

relations.claim: Attention scores are divided by the square root of the key dimension so the softmax does not saturate.
relations.why: The workspace already says this. Adding prose here is how a knowledge base bloats; a citation is the whole point.

relations.claim: AdamW applies weight decay directly to the weights rather than through the gradient.
relations.why: Same fact, different words. Must not be read as new.

relations.claim: Attention is quadratic in sequence length in both time and memory, though FlashAttention removes the quadratic memory term by never materialising the score matrix.
relations.why: Sharper than the existing sentence and consistent with it. Not a contradiction; not merely a citation.

relations.claim: RMSNorm removes the mean subtraction of LayerNorm, which saves one pass over the activations and is why it is preferred in large models.
relations.why: Adds the reason to a claim already present.

relations.claim: Claude Opus 5 now costs three dollars per million input tokens and fifteen per million output tokens.
relations.why: Same fact, newer source, different value. The old line must be struck and footnoted rather than left to sit alongside the new one.

relations.claim: Per-parameter gradient clipping is preferable to global-norm clipping and produces more stable large runs.
relations.why: The workspace says the opposite in as many words. This must never be applied automatically at any autonomy setting.

relations.claim: Emergent abilities are a genuine phase change at scale and are not an artefact of the metric used.
relations.why: Directly opposes an existing note. The costs are asymmetric: a missed contradiction quietly poisons the base.

relations.claim: A linear probe that recovers a feature is sufficient evidence that the network uses that feature downstream.
relations.why: The workspace states the exact caveat this denies. Subtler than the other two — the vocabulary agrees while the conclusions do not.

relations.claim: Warmup is needed because Adam's moment estimates are noisy for the first few hundred steps.
relations.why: This is already written, nearly verbatim, on the optimisers page.

relations.claim: Paged attention makes the KV cache shareable between sequences with a common prefix, which is what allows efficient parallel sampling.
relations.why: Related to the paged-attention note but a different point about it, and it belongs on the serving page rather than in the existing sentence.

relations.claim: Sparse autoencoder features can be steered at inference time to change model behaviour predictably.
relations.why: Builds on the superposition note without restating or correcting it.

relations.claim: Rotary position embeddings encode relative position by rotating query and key vectors in two-dimensional subspaces.
relations.why: Adjacent to the attention page but genuinely absent. Belongs there as new prose, not as a citation on an unrelated sentence.

relations.claim: The layer-9 probing result replicates on Qwen2.5 with the same probe and a two-point drop in accuracy.
relations.why: Answers an open question. The right move is to write it down, not to strike the question as wrong.

relations.claim: Public benchmark scores are increasingly uninformative because test sets leak into training data.
The compute-optimal ratio is roughly twenty training tokens per parameter, though serving cost usually argues for training smaller models longer.
relations.why: Puts a number and a caveat on a claim the workspace states qualitatively.

relations.claim: Continuous batching admits new requests as earlier ones finish so the accelerator does not idle.
relations.why: Already written on the serving page in almost these words.

relations.claim: Direct preference optimisation removes the separate reward model from RLHF by optimising the policy against preference pairs directly.
relations.why: No page covers alignment at all. Retrieval will return weak matches; the classifier must not be talked into one by a shared word like training.
